title: Keeping evidence without tipping off the attacker
body_md:
## Take the photo, then stop the car

After a minor road accident you photograph the scene before anyone moves the cars. An account takeover is different: the other car is still driving, and every minute spent framing the perfect shot is a minute it keeps going. Evidence does matter. It helps a bank understand a disputed payment, a provider investigate an account, and investigators link separate reports. It cannot by itself make a refund or a prosecution happen. For one person facing a live takeover, cutting off access and reporting a loss in progress usually matter more than watching the attacker for a “better” screenshot. Take a quick copy when it is safe, then contain.

### Build a small, private case file

Keep the original message or email, not only a cropped screenshot. For email, save the full message with its headers if the mail service lets you export it; a displayed sender name can be forged. Collect transaction references, the bank’s case number, account alerts, the relevant security activity, and dates with the time zone. Write a timeline that keeps what you observed (“19:10: saw transfer in bank app”) apart from what you infer (“may have started after the support call”). Where an entry is uncertain, mark it uncertain instead of filling the gap.

Take screenshots with enough context that a reviewer can tell which application and date they come from, and leave passwords, recovery codes and unneeded personal data out of any copy you share. Keep the originals in a private place, with a backup you control. Give a bank or an investigator only what they ask for, and only through a channel you have authenticated. The US IC3 asks complainants to keep originals secure, and its complaint form does not take attachments.

### What can disappear

Providers may rotate their activity logs, messages can be deleted, and resetting a device can wipe local evidence. If a work device or a serious malware investigation is involved, call the response team before you change anything; forensic handling is specialist work. Don’t try to get into the attacker’s account, “test” suspicious links, contact the attacker, or leave them logged in so you can watch. Note the alert, then revoke the sessions. Later, add confirmation letters and final outcomes to the same timeline.

widget_config.goal: Keep a usable private timeline and the original material, and still contain an active incident fast.
widget_config.today_action: Make an empty incident-note template with fields for date, time and time zone, observed fact, source, action, contact and case number. Store it privately.
widget_config.scope: General advice on organizing evidence. Legal admissibility and provider retention differ, and IC3 does not accept attachments to its complaint form, wherever the complainant lives and whatever their citizenship. The people in the examples are invented.

blocks.title: The log that may vanish
blocks.situation: Ada finds a device she doesn’t recognize listed in her email settings, along with a forwarding rule. She writes down the time and captures the security page, then revokes the sessions and deletes the rule.
blocks.analysis: A short record keeps the context without leaving access open. She holds on to the original alert and any export, privately, and does not send screenshots that show recovery details to friends.

blocks.title: The bank asks for a receipt
blocks.situation: Ben has phoned the number on his card, and the bank’s fraud team asks him for a transaction reference and a copy of a receipt, to be uploaded through its secure portal.
blocks.analysis: A real investigation may need material from him. Ben checks the channel independently, sends only the receipt asked for and records the case number. A rule of “never share evidence” would block a legitimate dispute.

blocks.title: A case file for a hijacked mailbox
blocks.setup: An invented case: a mailbox shows an unfamiliar forwarding rule, and a bank notice has arrived. You have to keep what is useful as evidence while stopping the access.

steps.prompt: You have found the forwarding rule. What do you record first?

choices.text: A short timeline, the alert and the visible rule, with dates and sources.
choices.consequence: You keep the context before the settings change.
choices.explanation: Separate what the account shows from what you suspect.

choices.text: Nothing written; you trust your memory.
choices.explanation: A record made at the time is worth more.

steps.prompt: A session you don’t recognize is still active. What next?

choices.text: Keep it connected for several days to watch it.
choices.consequence: More of your mail is exposed.
choices.explanation: An ordinary user should not trade containment for speculative evidence.

choices.text: Revoke sessions through the provider and secure the account; save any logs you can still reach afterwards.
choices.consequence: The attacker loses a way in while your records stay organized.

steps.prompt: An unsolicited “investigator” asks you to upload your whole mailbox. What do you do?

choices.text: Decline, and use a verified channel at your bank, provider or authority, sending only what is required.
choices.consequence: Other people’s mail and your own secrets stay private.
choices.explanation: Evidence has to travel through an authenticated channel, and only the necessary part of it.

choices.text: Upload everything to the link they sent.
choices.consequence: Sensitive material may land with another scammer.
choices.explanation: An unsolicited link is not an evidence channel.

steps.prompt: You can’t say when the rule first appeared. How do you show that in the timeline?

choices.text: Mark the time as unknown and note what is confirmed.
choices.consequence: A later reviewer can tell fact from inference.
choices.explanation: An honest gap beats invented precision.

choices.text: Pick a plausible time so the report looks complete.

blocks.debrief: Keep the originals and a factual timeline, shut down the live access, and send on only what is needed through verified channels. Go back and take the other choices; no screenshot is a substitute for stopping the harm.

blocks.title: The same habits, a different case

questions.prompt: A payment-app receipt shows a transfer. Which record is the most useful?

choices.text: The receipt plus the reference, the time, the app account and your report number.
choices.explanation: With these details the provider can identify the transaction.

choices.text: Only a cropped image of the logo.
choices.explanation: It cannot reliably identify the payment.

questions.prompt: Does the US IC3 complaint form accept your evidence attachments?

choices.text: Yes; upload all your files with the complaint.
choices.explanation: IC3 says it does not accept attachments.

choices.text: No. Keep the originals securely, for an agency that may ask for them later.
choices.explanation: That is the advice in the IC3 FAQ.

questions.prompt: A work laptop may need forensic review. What do you do before wiping it?

choices.text: Ask the organization’s response team and follow its procedure.
choices.explanation: Specialists can balance evidence against containment.

choices.text: Wipe it at once, to hide the event.
choices.explanation: That can destroy evidence and break procedure.
